playground.title: 1. Indexing Playground: Run NumPy Code, See Every Index
playground.intro: Write NumPy code below. It runs instantly in your browser, and every indexing operation is traced: which cells are picked, whether you get a view or a copy, and what else changes when you write.
playground.shortcut: Ctrl/⌘ + Enter · runs automatically as you type
playground.subset: Supported: one statement per line: assignment, slicing, integer/boolean indexing, arithmetic, print(), common np.* functions and array methods. Not supported: for / if / def.
playground.no_output: (no output; end with an expression such as a[1:3] to display it)
playground.no_ops: No indexing yet. Try adding a line like a[1:3, ::2].
playground.why_view: Only basic indexing (integers, slices, None, ...). NumPy just computes a new offset and strides over the same memory, so nothing is copied. Writing to the result changes {{target}}.
playground.why_fancy: An integer array index triggers advanced indexing: the elements are gathered one by one into a new buffer. Changing the result never affects {{target}}.
playground.why_mask: A boolean mask picks the positions where it is True, in row-major order, and gathers them into a new 1-D copy. Changing the result never affects {{target}}.
playground.why_scalar: Every axis is indexed by an integer, so you get a single scalar value instead of an array.
playground.why_write: Assignment writes straight into {{target}}'s memory at the highlighted positions. This holds for slices, fancy indexes and masks alike: a[mask] = 0 modifies a in place.
playground.adv_front: The advanced indices are separated by a slice, so their broadcast dimension moves to the front of the result shape.

note.newaxis: None: inserts a new axis of length 1

playground.memory_view: The result reuses this buffer: offset {{offset}}, strides {{strides}} (in elements).
playground.memory_copy: The result lives in a new buffer:
playground.alias_desc: {{name}} shares memory with {{target}}, so this write also changed {{count}} of its cells.
playground.too_large: Too large to draw (shape {{shape}}). Try a smaller array.
playground.hover_hint: Hover or tap any cell to see where it comes from. The small numbers give the order of elements in the result.

broadcast.title: 2. Broadcasting: Combining Arrays of Different Shapes
broadcast.intro: Broadcasting lets NumPy compute A + B even when the shapes differ, without copying any data. Choose two shapes, walk through the rule one axis at a time, and see which value each result cell uses.

story.outer: A column (3,1) meets a row (1,4): each side stretches along its length-1 axis and they fill a 3×4 grid.
story.row: Subtract one value per column from every row. This is how X − X.mean(axis=0) centers each feature.
story.scalar: A scalar has shape (), so it broadcasts to any shape: every element is multiplied by the same number.
story.mismatch: Trailing axes 4 and 3 differ and neither is 1, so NumPy raises an error. See the suggested fix below.
story.silent: Looks like adding two 3-element vectors, but (3,) acts as a row and (3,1) as a column, so the result is 3×3. No error is raised.
story.cube: B (3,1) is stretched along the last axis and repeated for both blocks of A.

broadcast.rule_title: Step 1 · Check the shapes axis by axis (right to left)

narr.align: Write {{a}} and {{b}} right-aligned. If one shape has fewer axes, pad it with 1s on the left (marked 1⁺). Then compare one column at a time, starting from the last axis.
narr.equal: Axis {{axis}}: both lengths are {{a}}. They are equal, so the result also has length {{out}} here.
narr.stretchA: Axis {{axis}}: A has length 1, B has {{b}}. A's single value is reused {{out}} times along this axis.
narr.stretchB: Axis {{axis}}: B has length 1, A has {{a}}. B's single value is reused {{out}} times along this axis.
narr.mismatch: Axis {{axis}}: {{a}} vs {{b}}. They differ and neither is 1, so broadcasting fails here.
narr.done_ok: Every axis is compatible, so the result shape is {{shape}}.
narr.done_fail: Incompatible at axis {{axis}}: NumPy raises a ValueError.

broadcast.visual_title: Step 2 · See the stretch: both operands viewed as {{shape}}
broadcast.hover_hint: Hover or tap any cell to see which A and B values it combines.
broadcast.memory_desc: A stride of 0 means moving along that axis re-reads the same element, so the stretched operands are free. Only {{a}} + {{b}} values are stored; NumPy allocates memory just for the {{out}}-element result.
broadcast.error_title: operands could not be broadcast together
broadcast.fix: Fix: add a length-1 axis, turning {{from}} into {{to}}:

cards.rule_1: Line the shapes up on the right.
cards.rule_2: Compare each axis: the lengths must be equal, or one of them must be 1.
cards.rule_3: A missing axis counts as 1. The result takes the larger length on each axis.
cards.mem: A length-1 axis is stretched by giving it stride 0, which re-reads the same value instead of copying it. Code like X - mu is therefore both shorter and faster than a Python loop.
cards.ml_t: Where you'll meet it in COMP2211
cards.ml_bias: add the same bias to every sample
cards.ml_knn: all pairwise differences for KNN distances
cards.pit: A 1-D array of shape (3,) behaves like a row. Combining it with a (3,1) column gives a 3×3 matrix instead of 3 values, and NumPy raises no error. Check .shape, and write a[:, None] or a.reshape(-1, 1) when you mean a column.

broadcast.advice: Broadcasting doesn't actually copy data in memory, but virtually maps addresses during iteration. Core rule: Compare from the last dimension forward, they must either be equal or one of them is <1>1</1>.

pairwise.title: 3. Pairwise Distance in One NumPy Line (Exam Video)
pairwise.intro: A short animated video on a question that keeps coming back in COMP2211 papers: compute every test-to-train distance with no loops. It uses the exact data from the 2022 Spring midterm Q2(c) and follows the official marking scheme, tracking the shape at every step.
pairwise.video_label: Video: pairwise distance in one NumPy line
pairwise.keys: Click the video to play or pause. Keyboard: Space plays or pauses, ← / → move between scenes. Click a chapter to jump to it.
pairwise.code_title: Try it: the same steps, run by the in-browser interpreter
pairwise.advice: Every year this shows up as KNN or K-Means "without loops": 2022S Q2(c) for Euclidean distance, 2023F for Minkowski + np.argsort(…, axis=1)[:, :k], 2023S for a Poincaré distance with np.expand_dims. Marks go to the shape change, the right axis in sum / argsort, and the (num_test, num_train) order. Write the shape as a comment after every step; that alone catches most mistakes.

question.title: The exam question
question.c1: This exact task was in the COMP2211 2022 Spring midterm (Q2c, 9 points): rewrite a nested-loop distance function with no explicit loops.
question.c2: The marking scheme is blunt: any for loop or list comprehension scores 0. You need the one-line broadcasting trick.
question.c3: Here is the answer we are going to build. Let's take it apart and track the shape at every step.

data.title: What we want
data.c1: X_test holds 2 points and X_train holds 4, each with 2 coordinates: shapes (2, 2) and (4, 2).
data.c2: We need the distance between every test point and every train point: 2 × 4 = 8 numbers.
data.c3: Row i is test point i and column j is train point j, so the answer has shape (num_test, num_train) = (2, 4). Getting it the wrong way round costs a mark.

line.title: The one line
line.c1: Read it from the inside out: five operations, and only the first one is tricky.
line.c2: The shape goes (2, 2) & (4, 2) → (2, 4, 2) → (2, 4). The 3-D middle step holds all 8 pairs at once.

fail.title: Why X_test − X_train fails
fail.c1: First instinct: just subtract. NumPy compares shapes from the right, and the last axis is fine: 2 vs 2.
fail.c2: But then 2 test rows meet 4 train rows. They differ and neither is 1, so NumPy raises a ValueError.
fail.c3: If the counts happened to match, it would be worse: no error, just the wrong pairs. Under the marking scheme, no shape change scores 0 of the 4 subtraction points.

axes.title: Insert a new axis
axes.c1: The fix is to give each array its own axis. None (= np.newaxis) inserts an axis of length 1 where you write it.
axes.c2: X_test[:, None, :] is (2, 1, 2), with test points down axis 0. X_train[None, :, :] is (1, 4, 2), with train points along axis 1.
axes.c3: Broadcasting will stretch the 1s. np.expand_dims(X_test, 1) does the same thing, and X_train[None] is optional because NumPy pads missing axes on the left.

broadcast.title: Broadcast: (2, 4, 2)
broadcast.c1: Compare (2, 1, 2) with (1, 4, 2): the last axes match, and in each of the other two one side is 1. Both arrays can stretch.
broadcast.c2: Test points are reused across the 4 columns and train points down the 2 rows. Nothing is copied in memory: the stretched axis has stride 0.
broadcast.c3: Cell [i, j] now holds X_test[i] − X_train[j]. That is all 8 difference vectors at once, shape (2, 4, 2).

reduce.title: Square, then sum axis = −1
reduce.c1: Square every coordinate difference: (5, 5) becomes (25, 25). The shape stays (2, 4, 2).
reduce.c2: Sum along the last axis, the coordinate axis, so each cell collapses to one number: (2, 4, 2) → (2, 4).
reduce.c3: axis=2 and axis=-1 are both right. axis=1 adds up different train points and gives (2, 2): it runs, but the result means nothing. The scheme deducts a point for a missing or wrong axis.

result.title: sqrt → the distance matrix
result.c1: Apply np.sqrt element by element. The shape stays (2, 4), and these are exactly the numbers printed in the exam paper.
result.c2: Row i lists test point i's distance to every train point, so KNN takes np.argsort(D, axis=1)[:, :k]. The 2023 Fall midterm asked exactly this, with Minkowski distance.
result.c3: Here train point r3 at (3, 4) is the nearest neighbour of both test points.

recap.title: Exam checklist
recap.c1: This is the shape trail. In the exam, write it as comments next to your code.
recap.c2: Check each item before you hand in. Most lost marks come from a missing axis or the wrong axis.
recap.c3: The (n, m, d) middle array is the price of the one-liner. Now run the code yourself below.

data.cell: D[i, j] = distance(test i, train j)

fail.silent: Silent trap: with 4 test and 4 train points, X_test − X_train runs without error but only pairs row i with row i, giving 4 differences instead of 16.

axes.pad: missing axes are padded on the left

broadcast.ghost: Dashed = virtual copies made by broadcasting (stride 0)

reduce.trap: Square the difference: (a − b)², not a² − b² (−3 points in the scheme).

result.match: matches the output printed in the exam paper

recap.no_loop: No for loop and no list comprehension, or the answer scores 0
recap.axis: Insert the axis: X_test[:, None] or np.expand_dims(X_test, 1)
recap.square: Square the difference (a − b)², not a² − b²
recap.sum: Sum over the last axis: axis=-1 (or 2)
recap.memory: Memory: the (n, m, d) intermediate costs n·m·d numbers. For large data, the official solution expands ‖x − y‖² = ‖x‖² + ‖y‖² − 2x·y and uses one matrix product, X_test @ X_train.T, so no 3-D array is ever built.

backprop_module.title: Chain Rule Tracker
backprop_module.step2_desc: Let <1>\delta_k = - \frac{\partial E}{\partial net_k}</1>. Under MSE loss:
backprop_module.advice: Remember, backpropagation is essentially a process of 'finding the culprit'. Each layer weight <1>w_{jk}</1> is asking: How much of the error <3>E</3> am I responsible for? <5>\delta_k</5> is the 'blame letter' passed back from the previous layer.
backprop_module.history_hint: Click 'Apply update' repeatedly: each gradient-descent step (w ← w + Δw) lowers E. Moving a slider starts a new run.
backprop_module.sigmoid_note: With sigmoid activation the derivative has a closed form:
backprop_module.diagram_label: Neuron diagram: inputs i and j feed output k through weights w_ik = {{wik}} and w_jk = {{wjk}}. Output O_k = {{out}}, target T_k = {{target}}.

kernel_module.advice: A convolution kernel is essentially a local feature filter. When you use the <1>\text{Laplacian}</1> operator, it is approximating the second derivative and can quickly capture 'sudden changes' in pixel brightness.

terms.prior_desc: Probability of belief <1>B</1> before any evidence.
terms.likelihood_desc: Probability of evidence <1>E</1> given belief <3>B</3> is true.
terms.marginal_desc: Total probability of evidence <1>E</1> under all conditions.

fire_case.title: 2. Practice: Smoke & Fire Case (Notes P.15)
fire_case.advice: Classic case from notes: Fire is rare (Prior=1%), but smoke is common (Marginal=10%, maybe BBQ). Bayes tells us probability of fire given smoke is only <1>9\%</1>. <3>Evidence ≠ Conclusion, Prior matters!</3>
fire_case.evidence_bound: By total probability <1></1>, so P(Smoke) cannot go below P(Smoke|Fire)·P(Fire) = {{v}}% — otherwise the posterior would exceed 100%.

naive.advice: Key point from Notes P.23: Bayes is 'Naive' because it assumes features are <1>conditionally independent</1>. Efficient for spam filtering. Watch out for <3>Zero Frequency Problem</3>, increase <5>\alpha</5> to see changes!
naive.zero_warning: A zero count makes the whole product 0 (log 0 = −∞), so that class can never win whatever the other features say. Increase <1></1> to smooth it away.

knn.click_instruction: Click background to move test point
knn.advice: Observe the interaction: As you increase <1>K</1>, the decision boundary becomes smoother. Small <1>K</1> leads to complex boundaries prone to <3>Overfitting</3> (capturing noise), while large <5>K</5> simplifies the boundary causing <3>Underfitting</3>. Also, toggle 'Standardized' to see how scale affects distance—without it, features with larger ranges (like Weight) dominate the distance calculation, which is a classic trap in KNN!
knn.canvas_label: KNN scatter plot. Click or use arrow keys to move the test point. Test point: height {{h}} cm, weight {{w}} kg. With K = {{k}} the prediction is {{cls}}.
knn.keyboard_hint: Tip: focus the plot and use the arrow keys to move the test point.
knn.loo_chart_label: Leave-one-out error rate for K = 1 to 15. Lowest error {{err}} at K = {{k}}.
knn.loo_hint: Real result, not a sketch: each of the {{n}} samples is held out and predicted by the others. Lowest error here: K = {{k}} ({{err}}). Green dot = best K, dashed line = your K.
knn.tie: Tie {{m}} : {{l}} — no majority, so the nearest neighbour breaks the tie → {{cls}}. Pick an odd K to avoid this.

exam_tip.title: Exam Tip
exam_tip.content_numpy: Exam Note: <1>Broadcasting</1> can only extend dimensions of Size 1. <3>A \cdot B</3> (np.dot) and <5>A \odot B</5> (Element-wise) have completely different physical meanings!
exam_tip.content_backprop: Exam Note: error flows backward — compute <1>\delta_k</1> at the output layer first. Memorize <3>\Delta w = \eta \delta O</3> and mind the sign of (T - O)!
exam_tip.content_kernel: Exam Note: with no padding and stride 1, output size is <1>N - K + 1</1>. Sobel-X responds to vertical edges — don't mix up the direction!
exam_tip.content_bayesBasics: Exam Note: <1>P(B|E) \propto P(B) \cdot P(E|B)</1>. The denominator P(E) only normalizes — compare hypotheses by the numerator!
exam_tip.content_naiveBayes: Exam Note: one zero frequency kills the whole product — apply <1>\alpha</1> smoothing. With many features, switch to <3>\log</3> sums to avoid underflow!
exam_tip.content_knn: Exam Note: choose an odd <1>K</1> to avoid tie votes, and always standardize features — otherwise large-range features dominate the distance!
exam_tip.content_alphabeta: Exam Note: pruning fires when <1>\beta \le \alpha</1>. Node visiting order matters — <3>a good move ordering prunes far more branches</3>!
exam_tip.content_kmeans: Exam Note: every iteration keeps <1>WCSS</1> non-increasing, so K-Means always converges — but only to a local optimum (initialization matters). Pick <3>K</3> at the elbow point!
exam_tip.content_perceptron: Exam Note: the update <1>w \leftarrow w + \eta\, y\, x</1> fires only on misclassified points — and converges only if the data is linearly separable!
exam_tip.content_pytorch: Exam Note: the training trio order matters — <1>\text{zero\_grad} \to \text{backward} \to \text{step}</1>. Forget zero_grad and gradients accumulate!

explain.leaf: Evaluate leaf {{node}}: static value {{value}}, return to parent {{parent}}.
explain.traverse: Descend from {{node}} to child {{child}}, carrying [α={{alpha}}, β={{beta}}].
explain.prune: β({{beta}}) ≤ α({{alpha}}) at {{node}} → prune! Skip remaining branches [{{children}}].
explain.exit: Exit {{node}}: final score {{value}}, return to parent.

alphabeta.advice: Alpha-Beta returns the exact same value as plain Minimax, just faster. The prune condition <1></1> means the parent already has a better guaranteed option, so the rest of this branch can never affect the result. <3>Move ordering is everything</3>: evaluate the most promising child first to trigger maximum pruning.
alphabeta.tree_label: Game tree with MAX and MIN nodes; colours show the active, visited and pruned parts at the current step.

kmeans.init_state: Initial state: points assigned to nearest of the initial centroids.
kmeans.moved: Centroids moved a total of {{d}} this step.
kmeans.elbow_hint: Inertia always drops as K grows; pick the 'elbow' where the marginal gain flattens.
kmeans.advice: K-Means alternates two steps (EM): assign each point to the nearest centroid, then move each centroid to its cluster mean. Inertia never increases. Choosing <1>K</1> is the hard part — use the <3>Elbow Method</3>. Always Z-score standardize first, or large-scale features dominate the Euclidean distance!
kmeans.canvas_label: K-Means scatter plot, K = {{k}}, iteration {{iter}}, inertia {{inertia}}.

perceptron.step_correct: Sample #{{idx}} correctly classified (target {{target}}) — no weight update.
perceptron.step_wrong: Sample #{{idx}} misclassified (predicted {{pred}}, target {{target}}) — update w += η·y·x, b += η·y.
perceptron.advice: The perceptron is error-driven: it only updates when it gets a sample wrong, nudging the boundary by <1>\delta = y - \hat{y}</1>. It is guaranteed to converge only if the data is <3>linearly separable</3>. Note the bias trick: merge <5>[w, b]</5> into one weight vector with a constant 1 input.

pytorch.autograd_subtitle: Drag inputs — forward computes values, backward fills gradients via the chain rule:
pytorch.autograd_hint: Each node stores data (forward) and .grad = ∂L/∂node (backward). ReLU passes gradient only when its input is positive — set a·b+c < 0 and watch all grads drop to 0.
pytorch.train_loop_hint: The sacred trio: zero_grad → backward → step. Forgetting zero_grad() makes gradients accumulate across batches.
pytorch.cnn_hint: Conv → Pool → Conv → Pool → Flatten → Dense. See the 'Kernel Lab' CNN tab for the layer-by-layer sizes.

api.tensor: Create a tensor; requires_grad enables autograd tracking.
api.create: Quick constructors for ranges and zero/one-filled tensors.
api.reshape: Reshape; -1 infers the dimension. Used to flatten before Dense.
api.device: Move model/tensor to GPU or CPU.
api.requires_grad: Track operations on this tensor to compute gradients.
api.backward: Run backprop; populates .grad on every leaf tensor.
api.relu: ReLU activation; Dropout randomly zeros units for regularization.
api.loss: Softmax + cross-entropy in one; pass raw logits.
api.optim: Stochastic gradient descent over model parameters.
api.zero_grad: Clear gradients BEFORE backward — or they accumulate.
api.step: Apply one gradient-descent update to the parameters.

pytorch.advice: The single most common bug: forgetting <1>optimizer.zero_grad()</1>. PyTorch *accumulates* gradients into .grad, so without clearing them each batch's gradient piles onto the last. <3>Order is fixed</3>: zero_grad → backward → step, every iteration.

rule.create: Builds a new array from scratch — there is no input array to trace.
rule.random: Fresh random values. The sandbox uses its own seeded generator, so the numbers differ from real NumPy, but the shape and range are the same.
rule.info: Returns a Python value rather than an array.
rule.move: Nothing is computed: every result cell is a copy of exactly one input cell. Hover to see which one.
rule.move_many: Nothing is computed: each result cell is copied from one of the {{n}} input arrays (tinted by origin).
rule.elementwise: Each result cell uses only the matching cell of each input. Shapes {{shapes}} are broadcast to {{out}} first.
rule.reduce_all: All {{n}} values collapse into a single number ({{op}}).
rule.reduce_axis: axis={{axis}}: the {{len}} values along axis {{axis}} collapse into one ({{op}}), so {{from}} becomes {{to}}.
rule.scan_flat: Running total over the flattened array: each cell is the sum of itself and everything before it.
rule.scan_axis: Running total along axis {{axis}}: each cell adds up everything before it in its lane.
rule.matmul: result[i, j] = row i of the left × column j of the right, multiplied pairwise and summed ({{k}} products).
rule.outer: result[i, j] = a[i] × b[j] — every pair, no summing.
rule.sort: Values are rearranged along axis {{axis}}; hover a cell to see where it came from.
rule.sort_flat: The whole array is flattened and sorted; hover a cell to see where it came from.
rule.argsort: argsort returns positions, not values: each number says where the k-th smallest value sits in the input.
rule.unique: Each distinct value once, sorted. Hover one to see every place it occurs.
rule.linalg: Every result cell depends on the whole matrix — there is no cell-by-cell shortcut.
rule.poly_create: A polynomial is just its coefficients, lowest degree first: [1, 2, 3] means 1 + 2x + 3x².
rule.poly_eval: Calling p(x) plugs x into the polynomial; the red dots are the values it returned.
rule.poly_deriv: The derivative (solid) is zero exactly where the original curve (dashed) turns around.
rule.poly_integ: The integral (solid) grows where the original (dashed) is positive and shrinks where it is negative.
rule.poly_roots: Roots are where the curve crosses zero. If it never crosses, the roots are complex and nothing can be marked.
rule.poly_convert: Fitted polynomials live on a shifted, scaled x; convert() rewrites them with ordinary x coefficients.
rule.poly_fit: Least squares: the curve that makes the total squared vertical gap to the points as small as possible.
rule.poly_arith: Polynomials combine with + − * ** like numbers; the solid curve is the result.
rule.polyfit: Legacy API: same least-squares fit, but the coefficients come back highest degree first.
rule.polyval: Legacy API: evaluates coefficients given highest degree first.

api.array: Turns a (nested) Python list into an array; the nesting depth becomes the number of axes.
api.arange: Evenly spaced integers like range(): the stop value is excluded.
api.linspace: A fixed number of evenly spaced points; both ends are included.
api.zeros: An array of a given shape filled with 0 (or 1 with np.ones); float unless you pass dtype.
api.full: An array of a given shape filled with one value.
api.eye: The identity matrix: 1 on the diagonal, 0 elsewhere.
api.zeros_like: Same shape and dtype as an existing array, but filled with 0.
api.reshape: Same values in the same order, new shape. Values are read row by row (C order).
api.reshape_neg: Put -1 for one axis and NumPy works out its length from the total size.
api.ravel: Flattens to 1-D in row order. ravel returns a view when it can; flatten always copies.
api.transpose: Swaps rows and columns: result[i, j] = a[j, i]. No data is copied.
api.swapaxes: Swaps two chosen axes of an N-D array.
api.expand_dims: Inserts a new axis of length 1 — the trick behind broadcasting a vector against every row.
api.concatenate: Joins arrays end to end along an existing axis; the other axes must match.
api.stack: Joins equal-shape arrays along a NEW axis, so the result has one more dimension.
api.vstack: vstack stacks rows on top of each other; hstack puts them side by side.
api.tile: Repeats the whole array like floor tiles.
api.repeat: Repeats each element (or row/column) in place.
api.flip: Reverses the order along an axis (all axes if none given). Returns a view.
api.slice: Basic slicing start:stop:step on each axis returns a view of the original.
api.fancy: Integer arrays pick arbitrary cells; paired lists give (row, col) points. Always a copy.
api.mask: A boolean array keeps the cells where it is True, flattened in row order.
api.where: np.where(cond, x, y) takes x where cond is True and y elsewhere, cell by cell.
api.broadcast: Arrays of different shapes combine after stretching length-1 axes — no copies are made.
api.scalar_op: Arithmetic with a scalar applies to every element.
api.compare: Comparisons give a boolean array, ready to use as a mask.
api.sqrt: Universal functions (ufuncs) apply to every element independently.
api.maximum: Element-wise larger of two arrays (or array and scalar) — np.maximum(z, 0) is ReLU.
api.clip: Limits every value to the range [low, high].
api.round: Rounds to the nearest value; exact halves go to the even neighbour (0.5 → 0, 1.5 → 2).
api.abs: Element-wise absolute value; np.square squares every element.
api.sum: Sums along one axis. axis=0 collapses rows (one result per column), axis=1 collapses columns.
api.sum_all: With no axis, every element is added into one number.
api.mean: Average along an axis — here one mean per row.
api.max: Largest value along an axis; np.min gives the smallest.
api.argmax: Position of the largest value along an axis — the predicted class for each row of probabilities.
api.std: Standard deviation along an axis. NumPy divides by n (ddof=0) unless you ask otherwise.
api.prod: Multiplies the values along an axis.
api.cumsum: Running total: each cell is the sum of everything up to it.
api.any: any: is at least one value True? all: are they all True? — along an axis.
api.count_nonzero: Counts the non-zero (True) cells — handy for counting correct predictions.
api.sort: Returns a sorted copy along an axis (the last axis by default).
api.argsort: Returns the indices that would sort the array — the core of KNN's nearest neighbours.
api.matmul: Matrix product: rows of the left times columns of the right. The inner lengths must match.
api.matvec: Matrix times vector: one dot product per row, e.g. a linear model's predictions.
api.outer: Every element of a times every element of b.
api.norm: Euclidean length: square, sum, square root — along an axis or over everything.
api.inv: Matrix inverse: A @ inv(A) gives the identity (up to rounding).
api.det: Determinant of a square matrix; 0 means it has no inverse.
api.rand: Uniform random numbers in [0, 1) with the given shape.
api.randint: Random integers from low (included) to high (excluded).
api.randn: Samples from the standard normal distribution (mean 0, std 1).
api.poly_note: The code block from this note, made runnable (q is defined here). Step through the calls to see each result.
api.poly_eval: Evaluate a polynomial at one value or a whole array at once.
api.poly_deriv: Differentiate (deriv) or integrate (integ) and get a new Polynomial back.
api.poly_roots: All roots of the polynomial, sorted; complex ones are returned as complex numbers.
api.poly_fit: Fit a polynomial of a chosen degree to noisy data, then convert() to read the coefficients.
api.polyfit: The old np.polyfit: coefficients highest degree first — for degree 1 that is [slope, intercept].

bayes.lead: A test that is 99% sensitive can still be wrong most of the time it says “positive”. The reason is the base rate: how rare the condition is in the first place.
bayes.again_text: <1>Test again.</1> Today’s posterior becomes tomorrow’s prior. Press it twice and watch a rare condition become likely.
bayes.grid_aria: Grid of 10,000 people coloured by group
bayes.answer_q: Among everyone with “{{evid}}”, how many really have “{{B}}”?
bayes.prior_was: Prior was <1>{{p}}</1>. The evidence multiplied the odds by <3>{{lr}}</3> (likelihood ratio P({{evid}}|{{B}}) ÷ P({{evid}}|{{notB}})).
bayes.base_rate_text: {{fp}} false alarms from the large healthy group swamp the {{tp}} true hits.
bayes.exam_text: Midterms give three numbers — a prior, P(E|B) and P(E|not B) — and ask for P(E) with the total-probability rule, then P(B|E) with Bayes’ rule. Watch for the twist: some papers ask for P(B | <1>not</1> E), which uses 1 − P(E|B) and 1 − P(E|not B). Switch “We observed” to try it.

course.note: Pattern of 2022 Spring Q3 — asks P(B | not E)

gnb.lead: When a feature is a number (temperature, score, pulse), Naive Bayes stops counting and fits one bell curve per class. The likelihood is the height of that curve at the test value.
gnb.curve_aria: Gaussian curve per class; click to move the test value
gnb.fit_title: Fit μ and σ per class
gnb.multiply_sub: P(class) × Π f(xᵢ | class) — P(E) cancels
gnb.predict_ratio: Predict <1>{{name}}</1> — its product is <3>{{ratio}}</3> the other class’s. Posterior = product ÷ sum of products; P(E) is the same for every class, so the exam only needs the products to decide.
gnb.predict: Predict <1>{{name}}</1>. Posterior = product ÷ sum of products; P(E) is the same for every class, so the exam only needs the products to decide.
gnb.traps: (1) The course uses the <1>sample</1> standard deviation, dividing by n − 1. (2) f(x) is a density, not a probability — it can be larger than 1 when σ is small. (3) In mixed tables, numbers use the Gaussian while categories still use counts (with Laplace smoothing if a count is 0).
gnb.naive_text: Each feature gets its own curve and the curves are simply multiplied. That assumes the features are independent given the class — the 2023 final asked what goes wrong when two features are strongly correlated.

lecture.title: Lecture 2: disease Z (continuous)
lecture.note: μ and σ given; BP = 66, Fever = 97

eval.lead: Accuracy hides which class the model fails on. Pick a class and the matrix splits into its true positives, false negatives, false positives and true negatives.
eval.labels_hint: Comma or space separated — or type straight into the matrix cells.
eval.rows_hint: The 2024 Spring midterm put <1>actual</1> on rows; the 2023 Fall midterm put <3>predicted</3> on rows. Read the axis labels before you sum.
eval.pr_question: Precision asks “when I say {{c}}, am I right?” Recall asks “of all real {{c}}, how many did I find?”
eval.gap: It is {{pts}} points above macro-F1 because one class dominates.
eval.mcc_random: MCC = {{mcc}} says it is close to a random guess.
eval.mcc_ok: MCC = {{mcc}} says it is still informative.
eval.agree: Accuracy and F1 agree here, so the classes are reasonably balanced.
eval.traps: (1) Which axis is actual? Precision divides by the <1>predicted</1> total, recall by the <3>actual</3> total. (2) Macro-F1 is the plain average of per-class F1 — not F1 of the averaged precision and recall. (3) On imbalanced data accuracy can be high while the rare class is never found; MCC and F1 expose it.

cv.lead: D-fold cross-validation cuts the data into D consecutive chunks. If the data is sorted by class and never shuffled, some training sets never see a class — and every test sample of that class is wrong.
cv.assumption: A test sample is correct if its class appears anywhere in the training folds, and wrong otherwise. That is all you need to explain the 0% / 50% / 100% results.
cv.order_sorted: x₀, x₁, … in the order given
cv.order_stratified: each class dealt evenly into the folds
cv.rounds: Each round: one fold tests, the rest train
cv.tip_unseen: test · class never seen in training ✗
cv.legend: Bright = test fold, faded = training. A dark underline marks test samples whose class never appears in training.
cv.how: For each D, write which classes land in each fold, say which training sets lose a whole class, and average the fold accuracies. Then give the fix: <1>shuffle before splitting</1>, or better, <3>stratify</3> so every fold keeps the class proportions.
cv.loo_title: Why D = number of samples always works here.
cv.loo: Leave-one-out leaves every other sample of the class in training, so with at least two samples per class the exam assumption never fails — the 2022 Fall paper made the same point about splitting an unbalanced dataset.

six.title: 6 patients, 2 classes
six.note: Pattern of Final 2024 Q3(b) — folds of 2 and 3

km.lead: Exactly the table the midterm asks for: distance from every point to every centroid, pick the nearest, average each cluster, repeat until no point changes cluster.

plane.title: Exam-style: 2-D, run to convergence
plane.note: Pattern of 2023 Spring Q5 — ties go to C1

empty.title: An empty cluster
empty.note: A bad seed can end up owning nothing

km.round_sub: ○ centroid used this round  ◆ new mean
km.table_note: Highlighted rows changed cluster since the previous round. Ties go to the lower-numbered centroid.
km.converged: In round {{r}} every point kept its cluster, so the means cannot move again. That is the sentence the marking scheme wants: “the cluster assignment remains the same”.
km.not_done: Press Next. K-Means stops only after a full round in which no point changes cluster ({{n}} rounds here).
km.not_done_never: Press Next. K-Means stops only after a full round in which no point changes cluster ({{n}} rounds here, without converging).
km.empty_note: One cluster ended up empty — a true/false favourite (2024 Spring: “possible” is True).
km.traps: Use the distance the question names — 2023 Fall wanted <1>squared</1> distances. Round only when the paper says so (usually 2 decimals). Ties go to centroid 1 unless told otherwise. K-Means always converges, but not necessarily to the best clustering: a different seed can give a different answer.
km.choose_k: Choosing k is not part of the algorithm. Exams ask for the elbow method: plot SSE against k and pick where the curve stops dropping sharply — not the k with the smallest SSE (that is always k = n).

perc.lead: Feed one row at a time: compute O, and only if it is wrong move w and θ by η(T − O)x. Watch the decision line jump until every point is on its side — or never, if no straight line exists.

course.title: Exam-style: course ratings
course.note: Pattern of 2022 Fall Q6 — f = 1 only if z > 0

pm.title: Exam-style: ±1 outputs
pm.note: Pattern of 2022 Spring Q6 — f = 1 if z ≥ 0 else −1

perc.plot_aria: Training points and the current decision line
perc.line_sub: blue side → output high · dashed = before this row
perc.start_text: Start: w = {{w}}, θ = {{theta}}, η = {{eta}}. Press <1>Next row</1>.
perc.converged: Epoch {{n}} made no changes, so every row is classified correctly. The data is linearly separable.
perc.no_conv: The weights keep changing. If no straight line can separate the classes (XOR), the perceptron rule never stops.
perc.epoch_note: An epoch has converged only when a <1>whole pass</1> makes no update — an exam answer of “not converged in 1 epoch” needs exactly that reason.
perc.activation: Papers disagree: lecture 5 and 2022 Spring output high when z ≥ 0, 2022 Fall only when z > 0, and outputs may be 0/1 or −1/+1. With −1/+1 outputs a mistake gives T − O = ±2, so the step doubles. Rows that land exactly on z = 0 are where students lose marks.
perc.separable: The perceptron convergence theorem: if a separating line exists, this rule finds one in finitely many updates. If none exists (XOR, or “success iff both ratings are 2 or 3” in 2022 Fall), you need a hidden layer — see the next page.

xor.lead: A single neuron draws one straight line, and XOR needs two. A hidden layer draws two lines, squashes the plane, and in the new (h₁, h₂) space one line is enough. Backpropagation finds those weights δ by δ.

hand.title: Hand-picked weights (step)
hand.note: Pattern of 2023 Spring Q7(c) / 2025 Spring Q7 — OR & NAND → AND

zeros.title: All weights zero
zeros.note: Final 2022 Q3(d): why zero init fails

xor.input_aria: Network output over the input plane
xor.step_title: No training with a step function.
xor.step_note: Its gradient is 0 almost everywhere, so backprop has nothing to follow (Final 2024 Q4c). The fix: a steep sigmoid σ(cx) approximates the step and still has a gradient.
xor.solved: All four points fall on the right side. Look at the hidden-space plot: the hidden layer moved (0,1) and (1,0) to one side of a single straight line — that is exactly what the 2023 Spring hint (“make the points linearly separable after the first layer”) asks you to construct.
xor.unsolved: Some points are still misclassified. Train more, or adjust weights by hand until the hidden-space plot becomes separable by one line.
xor.symmetric: Both hidden units have identical weights, so they always compute the same value and receive the same δ — they can never become different. This is why all-zero initialisation fails.
xor.hidden_delta_note: Hidden δ uses w5 and w6 <1>before</1> this step’s update, as on the lecture slides. With the lecture start, round 1 gives δk = 0.107022 and new w5 = 0.833245.
xor.loss_sub: ½(T − O)² averaged over the 4 samples
xor.overshoot: A very large η can overshoot and oscillate instead of settling.
xor.wb_note: every non-input neuron has one weight per input plus one bias
xor.traps: The course writes δk = (O − T)·O(1 − O) and <1>subtracts</1>: w ← w − ηδO. Some books write (T − O) and add — same result, but use the paper’s convention. With a <2>linear</2> activation, stacking layers adds nothing: the whole network collapses to one neuron (2022 Spring Q7b).
xor.output_note: Binary: 1 sigmoid unit. Multi-class: softmax over n units. Multi-label: n sigmoid units (Final 2022). Never ReLU at the output of a classifier: its range is unbounded, so there is no natural cut-off.

conv.lead: Slide the kernel over the padded image, multiply cell by cell, add up. Then answer the three things exams always ask: what padding does at the border, whether the kernel is flipped, and how big the output is.

stride.title: Exam-style: stride 2, padding 1
stride.note: Pattern of Final 2022 B Q1(a) — flipped vs not

reflect.title: Exam-style: reflect, then average
reflect.note: Pattern of Final 2022 A Q4(b) / Final 2024 Q5(c)

sharpen.name: Sharpen
sharpen.effect: boosts the centre against its neighbours

conv.slide_sub: click any output cell, or play
conv.fits: The window lands exactly on the last column and row.
conv.nofit_one: (n − k + 2p) is not divisible by the stride, so the last pixel is never covered. Exams floor the result — the lecture calls 7×7 with a 3×3 kernel and stride 3 “does not fit”.
conv.nofit_many: (n − k + 2p) is not divisible by the stride, so the last pixels are never covered. Exams floor the result — the lecture calls 7×7 with a 3×3 kernel and stride 3 “does not fit”.
conv.rounded: Final 2022 rounded averages to integers — check what the paper says.
conv.modes_title: The four padding modes on this image
conv.modes_sub: padding 2 so the pattern is visible
conv.modes_note: Final 2022 and Final 2024 called the edge-repeating version “reflection padding”. If a paper is ambiguous, write which one you used.
conv.range_title: Range of this kernel on an 8-bit image
conv.flip_note: Lecture 7’s formula O(x,y) = Σ K(m,n)·I(x−m, y−n) is true convolution, which rotates the kernel by 180°; lecture 8’s practice says “don’t forget to flip”. Final 2022 accepted both answers (73 unflipped, 27 flipped). Symmetric kernels give the same result either way.
conv.local_note: A 3×3 kernel only sees a 3×3 neighbourhood, so no kernel can flip a 64×64 image — a pixel’s new value would have to come from up to {{n}} pixels away (Final 2024 Q5e).

otsu.lead: A point operation changes each pixel on its own, so you can read its effect straight off the histogram. Otsu’s method picks the threshold automatically: split at T, average both sides, move T to the midpoint, repeat.

grid4.title: Exam-style: 4×4 grid
grid4.note: Pattern of Final 2022 A Q4(b)(iii) — start at the mean

otsu.stop_one: Stop when T stops changing — here after {{count}} iteration, at <1>T = {{T}}</1>.
otsu.stop_other: Stop when T stops changing — here after {{count}} iterations, at <1>T = {{T}}</1>.
otsu.why: It chooses T automatically from the histogram, so two people thresholding the same image get the same result (Final 2024 Q5b).
otsu.match_title: Match each image to its histogram

point.why: new value depends only on the old value

flip.why: the value comes from a different position

otsu.traps: Write which side of T a pixel equal to T goes to (here R1: ≤ T). Thresholding outputs only two values, so its histogram has two bars. A flip leaves the histogram untouched — that is how the 2024 final expected you to spot it.

cnn.lead: Every final exam has this table: the output shape and parameter count of each layer. Build any stack, see every number with its working, and compare it with an MLP on raw pixels.

same.title: Keras padding="same"
same.note: Final 2024 Q7(a): stride 2 halves the size

mlp.title: MLP on raw pixels
mlp.note: Final 2022 B Q1(f)(ii): count and compare

cnn.not_div: {{a}} is not divisible by {{s}}: red cells are never covered
cnn.slip_title: Spot the slip in the official answer.
cnn.slip: The 2022 marking scheme printed 13 × 13 for layer 4, but ⌊(27 − 3 + 2·1) / 2⌋ + 1 = 14. Thirteen is what you get if you forget the padding. Layer 5 is 7 × 7 either way, and the parameter counts do not depend on it.
cnn.strip_title: Where does the output size come from?
cnn.rules: Conv: (k·k·C<1>in</1> + 1) × filters — the depth of the input counts, the image size does not. Pooling, Flatten and Dropout have none. Dense: (inputs + 1) × units. The +1 is the bias; leave it out only if the paper says “no bias”.
cnn.why: One kernel is reused at every position (parameter sharing), and each output only looks at a small window (sparse connections). A dense layer needs a separate weight for every pixel — see the MLP preset. Changing the input size breaks the first dense layer unless a global pooling layer squeezes the map to 1 × 1 first (Final 2023 Q6f).

xor.title: Why XOR needs a hidden layer
xor.sub: One neuron draws one straight line. Watch a hidden layer bend the plane until one line is enough.

label.one_line: A single neuron: one straight line, output 1 on one side.
label.blue_side: Shaded side → output 1. Yellow rings mark mistakes.
label.dont_bend: Don’t bend the line. Move the points.
label.hidden_moves: The hidden layer gives every point new coordinates (h₁, h₂).
label.lines_stay: Straight lines stay straight, parallel lines stay parallel.
label.still_stuck: Still no line separates them: a linear map alone cannot help.
label.into_square: Every point is squeezed into the unit square — and the plane is now bent.
label.one_line_now: In hidden space a single straight line does the job.
label.pulled_back: That one line, seen back in the input plane
label.band: is a curved band around (0,1) and (1,0). Two hidden lines, one non-linear boundary.
label.trap_linear: Trap: with a linear activation, extra layers add nothing — the whole network is still one line.

title.title: Introduction
title.c1: Exam after exam asks the same question: why can a single perceptron not learn XOR, and what does a hidden layer change?

points.title: Four points
points.c1: XOR has just four inputs. It outputs 1 when exactly one of x₁, x₂ is 1 — blue — and 0 otherwise — red.
points.c2: Put them on the plane: the blue points sit on one diagonal, the red points on the other.
points.c3: A single neuron computes step(w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b). Its boundary w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b = 0 is one straight line.

lines.title: Try every line
lines.c1: So let us try lines. Every position, every angle.
lines.c2: Some get two points right, many get three. Watch the best score.
lines.c3: It never reaches four. Three out of four is the best any straight line can do.
lines.ponder: Before the next chapter: can you prove no line works, using only four inequalities?

proof.title: The four-line proof
proof.c1: Write down what each point demands from w₁, w₂ and b.
proof.c2: (0,0) must give 0, so b ≤ 0. The two blue points need w₁ + b > 0 and w₂ + b > 0.
proof.c3: Add those two: w₁ + w₂ + 2b > 0, so w₁ + w₂ + b > −b, which is at least 0.
proof.c4: But (1,1) must give 0, so w₁ + w₂ + b ≤ 0. Contradiction. This is the full-mark answer to 2025 Spring Q7(c).

idea.title: Change the question
idea.c1: If no line fits the points, change the points. That is exactly what a hidden layer does.
idea.c2: Each hidden neuron computes a new coordinate. The output neuron then draws its line in that new space, not in the original one.

stretch.title: Step 1: a linear map
stretch.c1: First the weights: z = 3(Wx + c). Watch the whole grid move with it.
stretch.c2: A linear map can stretch, shear and shift the plane…
stretch.c3: …but straight lines stay straight and parallel lines stay parallel.
stretch.c4: So the points are still not separable. A linear step alone changes nothing — which is why the activation matters.

squash.title: Step 2: the sigmoid squash
squash.c1: Now the activation. σ squeezes every number into the range 0 to 1.
squash.c2: Applied to both coordinates, it squashes the stretched plane into the unit square. The grid lines bend.
squash.c3: The red point (1,1) is pushed to the top-right corner, (0,0) to the bottom-left edge, and both blue points end up near the bottom right.

separate.title: Step 3: one straight line
separate.c1: Here are the four points in hidden space, with their new coordinates.
separate.c2: The output neuron draws one straight line: y = step(h₁ − h₂ − 0.4).
separate.c3: Both blue points are on one side, both red points on the other. XOR solved.
separate.c4: Look at the corners: h₁ behaves like OR, h₂ like AND, and the output says “OR but not AND” — which is XOR.
separate.ponder: Why does the activation have to be non-linear? What would happen to the bent grid without σ?

pullback.title: Back in the input plane
pullback.c1: Let us carry that straight line back through the network: undo the squash…
pullback.c2: …undo the stretch, and colour every input by the network’s answer.
pullback.c3: The straight line in hidden space becomes a curved band in the input plane. That non-linear boundary is what a single neuron could never draw.

exam.title: The exam version
exam.c1: Exams often want the weights by hand with step activations. One standard answer: h₁ = OR, h₂ = NAND, output = AND.
exam.c2: Check the table row by row: only (0,1) and (1,0) make both hidden units fire.
exam.c3: And a classic trap: stack linear layers and you get W₂W₁x — still one linear function, still one line. The non-linearity is the whole point.

recap.title: Recap
recap.c1: Three things to remember for the exam.
recap.c2: Next: try the XOR page, where you can train this network with backpropagation step by step.

recap.1: One neuron = one straight line. XOR’s four inequalities contradict each other.
recap.2: A hidden layer moves the points: linear map, then a non-linear squash.
recap.3: In hidden space one line separates them; pulled back, it is a curved boundary.

points.1: Prove “a single perceptron cannot learn XOR” with the four inequalities: b < 0, w₁ + b > 0, w₂ + b > 0, w₁ + w₂ + b < 0.
points.2: Two hidden neurons are enough. A common hand answer is OR and NAND feeding an AND.
points.3: Without a non-linear activation, any number of layers collapses into one linear layer.
points.4: “Make the points linearly separable after the first layer” — sketch the hidden-space picture to show it.

exam.q: Network A is a single perceptron, Network B adds one hidden layer with two neurons. Show that A cannot learn XOR, and give weights with which B can.
exam.a: A: (0,0)→0 needs b < 0; (0,1), (1,0)→1 need w₂ + b > 0 and w₁ + b > 0, so w₁ + w₂ > −2b; (1,1)→0 needs w₁ + w₂ < −b < −2b. Contradiction. B (step units): h₁ = step(x₁ + x₂ − 0.5), h₂ = step(−x₁ − x₂ + 1.5), y = step(h₁ + h₂ − 1) with output 1 only when the sum is > 0.
